::: {.hidden}
$$
\newcommand{\expr}[3]{\begin{array}{c}
#1 \\
\bbox[lightblue,5px]{#2}
\end{array} ⊢ #3}
\newcommand{\ct}[1]{\bbox[font-size: 0.8em]{\mathsf{#1}}}
\newcommand{\abbr}[1]{\bbox[transform: scale(0.95)]{\mathtt{#1}}}
\def\true{\ct{T}}
\def\false{\ct{F}}
$$
:::

Let's consider the two sentences in (@ex-showed), which, arguably, entail each other.

(@ex-showed) a. Frodo showed the ring to Sam. <br>
	b. Frodo showed Sam the ring.

To capture this mutual entailment, we might assign the ditransitive verb *showed* two distinct lexical entries, as in (@ex-showed-lexicon).

(@ex-showed-lexicon) $⟨\textit{showed}_{1}, (λx.(λy.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))⟩ ⊢ (((np\backslash s)/pp)/np)$ <br>
	$⟨\textit{showed}_{2}, (λy.(λx.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))⟩ ⊢ (((np\backslash s)/np)/np)$

We can also assign a lexical entry to the preposition *to*, according to which it is interpreted as the *identity function* $(λx.x)$.
This interpretation for the preposition makes it *semantically vacuous*:
it simply takes an entity argument ($x$) and spits it right back out.

(@ex-to-lexicon) $⟨\textit{to}, (λx.x)⟩ ⊢ (pp/np)$

Recall that the semantic type of prepositional phrases ($pp$) is $e$.
As a result, the semantic type of *to* is $(e → e)$.

According to the first lexical entry for *showed*, the verb combines with an object noun phrase;
then it combines with a prepositional phrase;
and then it combines with a subject noun phrase, yielding, e.g., (@ex-showed\-a).
According to the second, it combines with an indirect-object noun phrase;
then a direct-object noun phrase;
and then the subject, yielding, e.g., (@ex-showed\-b).

A derivation of the (@ex-showed\-a) sentence would go:

$$\begin{prooftree}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{Frodo}, \ct{f}⟩ ⊢ np\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{showed}_{1}, (λx.(λy.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))⟩ ⊢ (((np\backslash s)/pp)/np)\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{the ring}, \ct{r}⟩ ⊢ np\)}
\RightLabel{\(/\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{showed\(_{1}\) the ring}, (λx.(λy.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))(\ct{r})⟩ ⊢ ((np\backslash s)/pp)\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{to}, (λx.x)⟩ ⊢ (pp/np)\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{Sam}, \ct{s} ⟩ ⊢ np\)}
\RightLabel{\(/\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{to Sam}, (λx.x)(\ct{s})⟩ ⊢ pp\)}
\RightLabel{\(/\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{showed\(_{1}\) the ring to Sam}, (λx.(λy.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))(\ct{r})((λx.x)(\ct{s}))⟩ ⊢ (np\backslash s)\)}
\RightLabel{\(\backslash\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{Frodo showed\(_{1}\) the ring to Sam}, (λx.(λy.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))(\ct{r})((λx.x)(\ct{s}))(\ct{f})⟩ ⊢ s\)}
\end{prooftree}$$

At the end of the day, we end up with the following truth value as the meaning of this sentence:

$$(λx.(λy.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))(\ct{r})((λx.x)(\ct{s}))(\ct{f})$$
$$⇒ (λy.(λz.\ct{show}(z, \ct{r}, y)))((λx.x)(\ct{s}))(\ct{f})$$
$$⇒ (λz.\ct{show}(z, \ct{r}, (λx.x)(\ct{s})))(\ct{f})$$
$$⇒ \ct{show}(\ct{f}, \ct{r}, (λx.x)(\ct{s}))$$
$$⇒ \ct{show}(\ct{f}, \ct{r}, \ct{s})$$

(It can be helpful to check and make sure you understand each line, as the above expression in our metalanguage is evaluated.)

Meanwhile, a derivation of (@ex-showed\-b) would go:

$$\begin{prooftree}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{Frodo}, \ct{f}⟩ ⊢ np\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{showed}_{2}, (λy.(λx.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))⟩ ⊢ (((np\backslash s)/np)/np)\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{Sam}, \ct{s}⟩ ⊢ np\)}
\RightLabel{\(/\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{showed\(_{2}\) Sam}, (λy.(λx.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))(\ct{s})⟩ ⊢ ((np\backslash s)/np)\)}
\AxiomC{\(⟨\textit{the ring}, \ct{r} ⟩ ⊢ np\)}
\RightLabel{\(/\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{showed\(_{2}\) Sam the ring}, (λy.(λx.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))(\ct{s})(\ct{r})⟩ ⊢ (np\backslash s)\)}
\RightLabel{\(\backslash\)}\BinaryInfC{\(⟨\textit{Frodo showed\(_{2}\) Sam the ring}, (λy.(λx.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))(\ct{s})(\ct{r})(\ct{f})⟩ ⊢ s\)}
\end{prooftree}$$

If we evaluate the result, we get:

$$(λy.(λx.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, y))))(\ct{s})(\ct{r})(\ct{f})$$
$$⇒ (λx.(λz.\ct{show}(z, x, \ct{s})))(\ct{r})(\ct{f})$$
$$⇒ (λz.\ct{show}(z, \ct{r}, \ct{s}))(\ct{f})$$
$$⇒ \ct{show}(\ct{f}, \ct{r}, \ct{s})$$

(Again, it is helpful to check each line.)

Thankfully, the sentence interpretation that results is the same in both cases.
Why "thankfully"?
As we saw, the two sentences entail each other.
To account for this fact, we should make sure they both end up true or false in the same situations---i.e., they should be given the same interpretation, regardless of what model we're considering.

And importantly, the analysis above derives this result precisely due to how we designed the lexical entries for prepositional-dative *show* and double-object dative *show*.
In particular, how we designed their meanings.
